const __out = [];
for (const [__i, __it] of $input.all().entries()) {
  try { __out.push(...(($input) => {

// Pick the report by Soul Urge, pick her versions, fill her lines. HOLD, never guess.
// Mirrors lib11_assemble.fill (check-11-assemble.py proves they match for every buyer).
const j = $input.first().json;
const T = {"9": {"cards": ["the-empress", "the-emperor", "the-fool", "the-high-priestess", "the-hanged-man", "the-hierophant", "the-lovers", "the-tower", "the-moon", "the-sun", "temperance", "strength"], "sections": {"opening": ["{{FIRST}},

Find somewhere to read this where nobody's going to walk in and ask what's wrong.

Read the cards in the order I turned them, and don't skip ahead to the letter at the end. It only comes back whole. Go straight to the last page and you'll get some words, and nothing else. A few of these cards will look like they're arguing with each other. Keep going anyway.

Two things before I start. This is someone living. And nothing in these pages asks you to contact them, wait for them or forgive them. If this person hurt you, you owe them no reply.

The night your order came in, I cleared the kitchen table and took three cards out of the deck: the Hermit, Judgement and the Devil. They'd said their piece, so they went up on the windowsill, and that left nineteen. I wrote {{BIRTH_NAME}} at the top of a clean sheet and {{DOB}} under it. Your birth name and date set how I lay your twelve cards. That's why they go down before anything else does.

Then I made a pot of mint tea and sat down with it. The one who came to me before was at my shoulder before I'd poured the first cup. No face and no voice, same as last time."], "1": ["**They took your softness, {{FIRST}}.**

You've felt the gap for a long time, and you've called it other things. Getting older. Getting wise to people. Being tired. I told you most women guess wrong, and that's how they do it: they name what the gap did to them, and never what used to be in it.

Here's what used to be in it. Your softness is the part of you that lets things reach you and lets you show. It runs both ways. Care comes in, and you let it land. Warmth goes out, and need goes with it, and you don't stop to check where it falls. When I told you about the old man on my windowsill holding his light up in the dark, and said the light was what they'd walked off with, I meant this.

The Empress sits right back among cushions in an open field. She isn't perched on the edge, ready to get up. Her whole weight's given over, and she's letting the cushions hold her.

You used to be like her with people, before them. Someone asked how you were and you told them the real answer, not the short one. You cried at the sad part of a movie with other people in the room and didn't care who saw. When a friend put an arm around you, you leaned into it instead of patting her back twice and moving off. If you missed someone, you picked up the phone and said so. When something stung, it showed on your face before you'd decided whether it ought to. You took a compliment and kept it. You let people do things for you, said thank you, and that was the end of it. None of it took any thought. It went in and out of you the way breath does.

Then it cost you. Someone made sure it cost you, and you learned so well that you shut it down in both directions at once, the coming in and the going out. You didn't sit down and decide to. You just noticed one day that you hadn't cried in front of anybody in a very long time, and you were a little proud of yourself for it.

When I turned this card, the one at my shoulder came in closer. I felt it on the back of my neck, the way you feel someone reading over you. They know exactly what they're holding.

I picked up my pen, looked at your name, and put the pen down again. The sheet had nothing on it but your name and your date.

The next time somebody asks how you are, notice what your face does before you answer. That quick, flat look that says fine is sitting right where your softness used to be."], "2": ["You don't call it a gap. You call it being strong.

Next came the Emperor, sitting square on a stone throne in a red robe, and at his arms and his legs you can see armor under the robe. He's dressed for a court and he's armed for a fight, and he never takes the second thing off.

Strong looks like this. Someone offers to help and you wave them away. Someone thanks you and you make a joke of it so it can't land. When you cry, you do it in the car or the shower, or you skip it. Nothing gets in and nothing gets out, and you've got a good word for that.

People tell you they admire it. They have no idea what they're praising. They're admiring a door you shut."], "3": ["You've asked yourself how you could have been so stupid. Put that question down, because it has the whole thing backwards. Being open isn't the same as being stupid.

They saw something in you: {{EX.saw}}. And they saw it came with your softness out in the open right beside it. Whatever you were good at, you did it warm. You let them see when you were pleased and when you were worried, and when you needed them. You didn't keep a guard on any of it, because you'd never had a reason to, and that's what made it easy to take. They knew what they were looking at. They went for it on purpose.

The Fool is a young man standing at the edge of a cliff with a white rose held loose in his lowered hand, stem down. He isn't gripping it or hiding it. Anybody who walked up could lift it out of his fingers.

You held yours like that. And they didn't take all of you. They kept {{EX.use}}, and they took the warmth that came with it. You went on giving them that after you'd stopped being soft with them, and that suited them fine. Whatever you gave, you gave honestly. Everything done with it after that is on them.

Why they've still got it comes next. For now I want one thing from you, and only one: stop asking what's wrong with you."], "4": ["They've kept it because giving it back means saying what they did.

The High Priestess holds a scroll with writing on it, and half of it is tucked under her mantle. She knows what the whole thing says. You only get to see part.

Handing your softness back would mean admitting it was never a weakness. And if it was never a weakness, then you were right, all along, and they were the one who made it look like a fault. While they hold on to it, they still get to be the person you thought they were. Give it back and that's gone. They didn't lose it and they didn't throw it away. They kept it covered."], "5": ["Why has this taken so long? Because they had one line that let them off, and the line was "She was too much."

The line held because your softness had been made to look like the problem. When you cried, it was a scene. When you needed something, you were needy. So "too much" sounded about right, even to you. It wasn't right. You were exactly as much as a woman who lets things reach her. They wanted less to deal with, and they called the difference your fault.

And you backed the line up without meaning to. Once you'd shut everything down and started calling yourself strong, you looked fine. Nobody had to ask what had been done to you, because there was nothing left to see. That was never your fault. You did what anyone does after being made to pay for something. Hiding behind it was their choice.

You still do their work for them, in small ways. You cut a story short at dinner in case it runs on. You say sorry before you ask for anything. You keep a bad week to one line in a text. Nobody has to shrink you now. You do it yourself, and you get there first.

On the Hanged Man, a man hangs head-down from a beam of living wood, tied by one ankle, and his face has no strain in it at all. He's settled in. They've been hanging off their line the same way, by one foot, calm, not looking at it.

The months I told you about, when they kept coming back to this, are that line wearing through. They have no idea it's happening."], "6": ["Here's their regret, plain: teaching you that going soft costs you.

Two ministers in white kneel on the Hierophant card with their backs to us, being taught. You can't see their faces. You can only see that they're taking the lesson in.

You took it in better than anyone meant you to. ", {"tag": "FORK", "opts": {"get_back": "And their regret isn't about losing you. It's about losing what they had from you, the warmth that used to come their way without being asked for. That isn't the same thing as you.", "giving": "They don't regret losing you, and they don't lie awake over it. If some part of you has hoped that somewhere they miss you, and would give anything to have you back, I won't let you go on hoping it. They don't."}}, " A regret like theirs pays nothing back and reaches nobody. You'll want to read it as love. It isn't."], "7": ["{{LP.then}}

It didn't stop when they left, though. Nobody switches a thing like that off. It kept running, and now it meets people who never laid a finger on you. Someone decent turns up and {{LP.now}}. One person set the price on your softness. It still gets charged to people who weren't there when it was set.

The Lovers are a man and a woman who stand close, but they aren't touching. He's looking at her. She's looking up and past him, at something over his head.

That's how it goes with the decent ones now. They're standing right there, close enough to touch, and your eyes go somewhere else before you've decided a thing. They offer you something warm and they meet the shut door, the one that was built for somebody else. None of them did a thing to you. And the warm thing they brought never gets to you either. They go home with it, and you're left with the door.

The next time someone kind says something kind to you, notice where your eyes go. If they go past the person, that's the old door, shutting on its own."], "8": ["Strong worked, {{FIRST}}, and you came by it honestly. Nobody's seen you fall apart. Nobody's had to carry you. You got up every day and did what needed doing.

Now here's what it did.

The Tower stands on bare rock with no door drawn anywhere on it, and lightning is coming down at it out of a dark cloud. Whoever built it made sure nobody could get in, and didn't think about how anyone inside was ever going to get out.

You built that after it ended, and back then it was the right thing to build. Here's what it's been charging you since. Every hand someone put on your arm that slid off before it could do you any good. Every time you said you were fine to somebody who'd have sat up with you half the night, and you spent that night by yourself instead. Every cry you saved until the house was empty, then did with the faucet running so even the walls wouldn't hear. Every piece of bad news you sat on until it was over, so nobody could fuss, and then told it later like a funny story. And the people who kept offering for a while and then quit, because they'd heard no so many times that they believed it. They didn't stop caring. They stopped asking, and you lost them without a word said on either side.

I got up from the table at that point, which I don't do in the middle of a spread. I went up to the upstairs window, because I could see what this card was doing and I needed a minute away from it. The street was dark and nothing moved in it. I stood there until my breathing settled, then came back down to the kitchen. It was past midnight. The lamp needed trimming and I let it smoke. The sheet was still blank under your name, and the one with no face had gone over by the door, as far from my shoulder as my kitchen goes.

Here's the deal, and I want you to have it exactly. Your softness comes back. The rest of this reading is how. The years you spent behind that wall don't come back. Nobody hands those over, not them, not me, not any card.

I told you it makes no difference to whether they've still got it, ten years or thirty. That's still true. But it makes all the difference to the bill. Years of birthdays where you smiled for the photo and went home and sat in the car. Years of being the one other people lean on, and leaning on nobody. Years of good people who got a polite version of you and never found out there was another one. Some of them would have stayed for the real one.

They made going soft expensive. That part is theirs, every bit of it, and I'm not taking it off them. Leaving the door off the tower made sense with them. It was never meant for the people who came after. It kept those people out anyway, every year it stood, and every one of those years went on your bill. They ran the bill up. You've been the one paying it."], "9": [{"tag": "FORK", "opts": {"get_back": "**They're trying to get you back, {{FIRST}}.**

And part of you is glad to hear it. Don't skip past that, and don't be ashamed of it either. I'm going to stay on it a minute, because of everything in these twelve cards, this is the part to watch closest.

After everything, the first place your softness wants to run back to is them. Some part of you still wants to be soft toward the one person who made it cost.

I won't dress that up for you. Give that part an inch and it starts making allowances. They must have changed, to be at this for months. They must be hurting too. You'd remember the good times first, and the rest a long way after. You'd find yourself being gentle about them in your head before you'd been gentle with one living soul in your own life. That's the danger, right there. The warmth you've refused everybody decent is still ready to go to them.

On the Moon, a path comes up out of the water, runs between two grey towers and goes off into the distance, and there's nobody on it. A dog and a wolf sit at the bottom with their heads up, howling at the moon, and nothing answers them. Nobody's coming down that path toward you, and nobody was ever going to.

Here's what their wish is really for. They don't want you. They want what used to come their way from you, pointed back at them again: the warmth, the way you let them land. They're holding your softness out with their hand open, waiting for you to walk all the way over and take it, so you'll be standing close enough to give it to them again.

They won't come down that path. A wish like theirs stays where it is and waits. It doesn't take a step.

I told you you'd need to know which way this went, because one way it's a gift and the other way it's a snare, and the words sound the same either way. It's the snare. Every kind thing in their letter is going to read like a reason to go to them. It isn't one.

I sat back down at the table, turned this card, and swore at my own hands for turning it. They didn't leave. They came right up to the table and stayed there, closer than they'd been all night. I'd have given a good deal to have them back over by the door. I kept my eyes on the card and off them. Three in the morning. Nine cards down, and the sheet was still blank under your name. I didn't know if I was going to get your letter at all.", "giving": "**They're giving it back, {{FIRST}}. They aren't trying to get you back.**

They want your softness out of their hands, and that's all the giving is. They've carried it a long time, and they're tired of carrying it. The line that let them off has worn through, and without it the thing has gotten heavy, so they're putting it down. They're doing it for their own sake. There's no love in it, and none of it is reaching for you. Once it's back with you, they can stop thinking about you. That's what they want out of this.

I told you one way this could go was a gift. This is that way, and it's colder than it sounds. It asks nothing because they want nothing from you: not your warmth, not an answer, not you.

On the Moon, a path comes up out of the water at the bottom of the card and runs away between two grey towers until you lose it. There's nobody on it, coming or going.

That path is the day you've kept free. You know the day I mean. They come to you. They sit down across from you and explain all of it, why they did what they did, in their own words, and you finally get to hear it out loud. You'd tell anyone who asked that you quit hoping for that a long time ago, and you'd believe it while you said it. Then some small thing would set it off again, and you'd catch yourself waiting.

You kept a place for it anyway. You shut your softness down with everybody, and somewhere underneath it all you left one small spot soft, just in case. It was for them, and for that day.

The day isn't coming. Nobody's going to walk up that path and sit down and explain. They aren't saving any of it for you, and on their side there's no place kept for you at all. What's in the letter at the end of these pages is everything you'll get from them. There won't be one word after it.

I'd sat back down to turn this one, and when it came up I cursed my own hands out loud. Then I looked over at the door. There was nobody by it. All night they'd been somewhere in my kitchen, at my shoulder or across the room, close enough that I'd stopped noticing, and now the room had only me in it. They'd gone. It was three in the morning. Nine cards down and three to go, your name at the top of the sheet and nothing under it, and whoever was carrying your letter had just walked out. I didn't know if I'd get it at all."}}], "10": ["**No, {{FIRST}}, they won't call, write or lift a finger about any of this, because {{REASON.headline}}.**

", {"tag": "REASON", "opts": {"0": "To do anything at all, they'd have to go soft in front of you and let it show. That's the very thing they made you pay for, and they won't pay it themselves.", "1": "You're that person. You saw what was done with your softness, up close, and being in a room with that is more than they can face.", "2": "You've paid for your softness every day since, and they haven't paid a cent. Nobody has ever sent them the bill."}}, " Don't go asking them for the reason. They couldn't give you one if you did. They're doing all of this without knowing it, and a person can't explain a thing they don't know they're doing. Asking would only hand them the pull again.

", {"tag": "FORK", "opts": {"get_back": "So they hold it out and they want you to come to them. I told you, back in the first letter, what it means when someone holds a thing out like that, and this is it. They won't take one step toward you. They want you to take all of them.", "giving": "So they're giving it back, and they still won't move. They'll let go of it right where they are, and that's all they'll do. They won't hand it to you, and they won't check that it reached you. As far as they're concerned, putting it down is the end of it."}}, "

Now the turn, and the whole reading hangs on it. They were never the ones who had to move. Your softness was never theirs to bring over to you in person, on a doorstep or down a phone line. It doesn't come back by contact, and it doesn't come back on their say-so. All it ever needed was for somebody to give up the wait.

The Sun shows a child riding bareback on a white horse, both arms wide open. Behind them, a low grey wall runs right across the card, and the horse is already out in front of it. Nobody opened a gate. Nobody came to let them out. They're past it, in full daylight.

You've been standing behind that wall waiting for them to come and open it. You've been waiting for them to say it, as if your softness needed their signature before you were allowed to have it back. Every time you've thought, if they'd only admit it, I could put this down, that was you standing at the wall. It never needed that. The day you stop waiting on their admission, it's already yours, the same way that horse is already past the wall without anyone's leave. Look at the card again. Nothing in it is waiting for anybody.

The window went from black to grey while I sat there. And I saw what I'd been doing all night. I'd been pulling at them for your letter, then sitting back and waiting for them to hand it over, and pulling again. The same thing you've been doing all this time. So I stopped. I said it out loud to my kitchen: I'm not waiting on you anymore.

", {"tag": "FORK", "opts": {"get_back": "Then they were across the table from me", "giving": "Then they were back, across the table from me"}}, ", in the chair where you'd sit, with the weight gone out of them. My pen moved. The first line of your letter was on the sheet."], "11": ["The sentence they never said is this: "You weren't weak. I made it expensive."

Don't answer it, not on paper and not in your head. You don't need to. By the time you've read it, it's already back.

Look at what it says. It names the price. It says that going soft was never the weak thing, and that somebody else set the cost on it. That's the thing you never once heard from them, and the thing you needed most. There it is, in their words. You can stop looking.

And you can stop writing their half. You've had them say sorry in your head, and you've had them say worse. You've given them lines on the bad nights and the good ones. You've run the whole talk over the dishes and lying awake, the one where they finally understand, and come out of it more tired than you went in. That job's finished. Their side is written down now, and it isn't yours to write. You'll notice the space it leaves. All the time that went into drafting what they'd say, you get those back.

You're about to read their words. If this person hurt you, you owe them no reply. Reading it is the whole of what you have to do.

On Temperance, a winged figure pours water from one cup into another, and the stream crosses the gap on a slant instead of dropping straight down. Their sentence got across to you like that, all of it, and nobody can take it back now."], "12": ["Stop going back to them, and once a day, let one thing show to someone safe. You'll get through what's coming on those two.

Your last card is Strength. A woman has both hands on a lion's mouth, closing its jaws gently. The lion's head is bowed. She has no whip and no iron, nothing but her two hands.

That's what strong was supposed to mean. Soft hands on something fierce, every day, and the fierce thing letting her. You've been using the word for a door with no gap in it. You can put that word down now. You don't need it.

The pull will be at its strongest now, inside the next five to seven days. That's about you, and what's moving in you. It says nothing about them turning up.

**Stop going back.** Rereading the old messages, looking them up, starting a message you swear you won't send: it's all the same thing. When the pull comes, put the phone in another room, set the oven timer for twenty minutes and keep your hands busy. Fold laundry. Wash a pan. Don't argue with it. Every one you let go by makes the next one smaller.

I told you the rereading stops. The need goes when you read the letter. The habit takes about a week, so your hand will still reach for the phone a few times. Let it.

**The one thing to do.** For seven days, once a day, let one thing show to someone safe. Tell a friend you missed her, in those words. When someone does something kind, let your face say so before you tidy it. When you're worn out and someone asks, say you're worn out. Only with people who've never given you cause. Nobody from your past.

You can't think your way back to softness. Small times that turn out fine do it, and if one goes badly, you'll find out you live through it.

It won't feel like much at first. You'll know it's working by what stops: your hand stops going to the phone late at night, and that flat look stops coming down so fast. How soon that happens is down to what you do with the twenty minutes and the seven days. It isn't down to me, and it isn't down to them.

", {"tag": "FORK", "opts": {"get_back": "Their letter ends with an ask. They want something from you in the last line. I've left it in. Do nothing with it.", "giving": ""}}, "

And the next time someone reaches for you, there's someone there.

Full light. After that first line, the rest of your letter came fast, and I could hardly get it down quick enough. I put the Hermit, Judgement and the Devil back in the deck. Then I wrote it out by hand at the same table, with them sitting across from me, and I didn't change a word of it.

Read it once, slowly, all the way to the end."], "letter": ["{{FIRST}},

I'm never going to send this. {{REASON.letter}} So it stays here.

I'll just say what I did. When you went soft on me, when you opened up or needed something, I made you sorry for it. I didn't always say anything. I didn't have to. You'd open up and I'd make you pay one way or another, and after a while you quit doing it. I saw that. I didn't do anything about it. Some of the time I was glad of it, because you were easier to be around when you weren't asking me for anything.

I'm not saying I planned it. I don't think I did. But it happened, and I let it.

When I first knew you, {{EX.letter}} I liked that. I liked having that around me. What I never said is you were warm with it. If you were happy, I knew. If you were worried, I knew. If you needed me, you said so, right out. I kept {{EX.kept}}. The rest I made you pay for.

I told myself you were too much. I said it to other people too. It was easier than the other thing, which was saying it was me. It doesn't work anymore. I still say it in my head sometimes and I can't get myself to buy it.

{{LP.letter}}

Why did I hang onto it? Because if I gave it back I'd have to own up. As long as I had it, I wasn't the one who did this. I knew that the whole time. I'm not stupid.

So here it is. I should have said it back then. I didn't.

You weren't weak. I made it expensive.

There was never anything wrong with you. It was the best thing about you, and I acted like it was costing me. It's your softness. It was yours before me and it's yours now. I'm giving it back. All of it. You don't owe me a thing for it.

", {"tag": "FORK", "opts": {"get_back": "Come back. Or if you won't, at least write me back.", "giving": "I'm not asking you for anything. Not to forgive me, not to see me, not an answer. Don't write to me, and don't go looking for me. That's all."}}], "close": ["When I looked up, the chair across from me was only furniture again, with nobody in it.", {"tag": "FORK", "opts": {"get_back": " I left their ask in so you'd see it for what it is. It's a bill, and nobody owes it, least of all you.", "giving": ""}}, "

It's back. What you do with it is on you."]}}};
